{{Short description|American condensed matter physicist (1929–2021)}}
'''Gene Frederick Dresselhaus''' (November 7, 1929, in [[Ancón, Panama]] – September 29, 2021, in [[California]])<ref name=Gale>biographical information from ''American Men and Women of Science'', Thomson Gale 2004</ref><ref name=obitMIT>{{cite web |url=https://news.mit.edu/2021/gene-dresselhaus-influential-research-scientist-solid-state-physics-dies-1109 |title=Gene Dresselhaus, influential research scientist in solid-state physics, dies at 91 |author=Halpern, Jane |website=MIT News, Massachusetts Institute of Technology |date= November 9, 2021 }}</ref> was an American condensed matter physicist. He is known as a pioneer of [[spintronics]] and for his 1955 discovery of the eponymous [[Dresselhaus effect]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Dresselhaus|first=G.|date=October 15, 1955|title=Spin–Orbit Coupling Effects in Zinc Blende Structures|journal=Physical Review|volume=100|issue=2|pages=580–586|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.100.580|bibcode=1955PhRv..100..580D}}</ref>

==Biography==
Dresselhaus studied physics at [[University of California, Berkeley]], receiving his bachelor's degree in 1951 and his doctorate in 1955. At Berkeley he worked under the supervision of [[Charles Kittel]] and [[Arthur F. Kip]] on early [[Cyclotron motion#Cyclotron resonance|cyclotron resonance]] experiments on [[semiconductor]]s and [[semimetal]]s.<ref>{{cite book|doi=10.1063/1.1993988|chapter=Personal Reminiscences of Cyclotron Resonance |title=AIP Conference Proceedings |year=2005 |last1=Dresselhaus |first1=G. |volume=772 |pages=7–10 }}</ref> As a postdoc Dresselhaus was for the academic year 1955–1956 an instructor at the [[University of Chicago]]. From 1956 to 1960 he was an assistant professor at [[Cornell University]]. He was also a consultant to [[General Electric]] Research Laboratories from 1956 to 1960 and to the [[Oak Ridge National Laboratory]] from 1958 to 1960. From 1960 he worked at the [[Lincoln Laboratory]] of the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT) and from 1977 at the Francis Bitter National Magnetic Laboratory of MIT. He was also a professor of physics at MIT.<ref name=Gale/>

He did research on [[carbon nanotube]]s, [[fullerene]]s, [[Band model|electronic energy bands]] in solids, surface impedance of metals, [[exciton]]s in insulators, electronic surface states, optical properties of solids, and [[high-temperature superconductivity]].<ref name=Gale/> 

In 1958 he married the physicist [[Mildred Dresselhaus]] (née Spiewak) — for many years the couple extensively collaborated and published their scientific findings. They had a daughter and three sons.<ref name="obitMIT" />

== Honors and awards ==
He was elected in 1966 a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]].<ref>{{cite web |title=APS Fellow Archive |url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1966&unit_id=&institution=Massachusetts+Institute+of+Technology+Lincoln+Laboratory |website=American Physical Society}} (search on year=1966 and institution=Massachusetts Institute of Technology Lincoln Laboratory)</ref> 

In 2022 he shared the [[Oliver E. Buckley Condensed Matter Prize]] with [[Emmanuel Rashba|Emmanuel I. Rashba]] for "pioneering research on spin-orbit coupling in crystals, particularly the foundational discovery of chiral spin-orbit interactions, which continue to enable new developments in spin transport and topological materials."<ref>{{cite web |title=2022 Oliver E. Buckley Condensed Matter Prize Recipient, Gene Dresselhaus |url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Dresselhaus&first_nm=Gene&year=2022 |website=American Physical Society}}</ref> His death in 2021 shortly preceded the announcement of the prize.<ref name="obitMIT" />
